prompts.L1:
Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

The layered structure and the rheological properties of anti-wear films, generated in a rolling/sliding contact from lubricants containing zinc dialkyldithiophosphate (ZDTP) and/or molybdenum dialkyldithiocarbamate (MoDTC) additives, have been studied by dynamic nanoindentation experiments coupled with a simple modelling of the stiffness measurements. Local nano-friction experiments were conducted with the same device in order to determine the evolution of the friction coefficient as a function of the applied pressure for the different lubricant formulations. For the MoDTC film, the applied pressure in the friction test remains low (<0.5 GPa) and the apparent friction coefficient is high ($\mu$ > 0.4). For the tribofilms containing MoDTC together with ZDTP, which permits the applied pressure to increase up to a few GPa through some accommodation process, a very low friction domain appears (0.01 < $\mu$ < 0.05), located a few nanometers below the surface of the tribofilm. This low friction coefficient is attributed to the presence of MoS2 planes sliding over each other in a favourable configuration obtained when the pressure is sufficiently high, which is made possible by the presence of ZDTP.

outputs.L1:
The layered structure and rheological properties of anti-wear films generated in rolling/sliding contact from lubricants containing zinc dialkyldithiophosphate (ZDTP) and/or molybdenum dialkyldithiocarbamate (MoDTC) additives were investigated using dynamic nanoindentation experiments, complemented by simple modelling of the stiffness measurements. Local nano-friction experiments were performed with the same device to determine the evolution of the friction coefficient as a function of applied pressure for the different lubricant formulations.  

For the MoDTC film, the applied pressure during the friction test remained low (<0.5 GPa), while the apparent friction coefficient was high ($\mu$ > 0.4). In contrast, for tribofilms containing MoDTC together with ZDTP, the applied pressure could increase to several GPa through an accommodation process, and a very low-friction domain emerged (0.01 < $\mu$ < 0.05), located a few nanometres below the tribofilm surface. This low friction coefficient is attributed to the presence of MoS₂ planes sliding over one another in a favourable configuration achieved when the pressure is sufficiently high, a condition made possible by the presence of ZDTP.
outputs.L2:
Dynamic nanoindentation tests, combined with a straightforward model for interpreting stiffness data, were used to investigate the layered organization and rheological behavior of anti-wear films formed in rolling/sliding contacts from lubricants containing zinc dialkyldithiophosphate (ZDTP), molybdenum dialkyldithiocarbamate (MoDTC), or both additives. Using the same instrument, localized nano-friction measurements were also performed to track how the friction coefficient changes with applied pressure for each lubricant composition.

In the film produced with MoDTC alone, the pressure reached during friction testing stays relatively small, below 0.5 GPa, while the measured apparent friction coefficient remains high, with $\mu$ greater than 0.4. In contrast, when the tribofilms contain both MoDTC and ZDTP, an accommodation mechanism allows the applied pressure to rise to several GPa. Under these conditions, a region with extremely low friction develops, with $0.01 < \mu < 0.05$, positioned a few nanometers beneath the tribofilm surface. This reduced friction is explained by MoS2 layers sliding against one another in an advantageous arrangement, which forms only once the pressure is high enough—a condition enabled by the presence of ZDTP.
outputs.L3:
The study investigated the layered structure and rheological behavior of anti-wear tribofilms formed from lubricants containing zinc dialkyldithiophosphate (ZDTP) and/or molybdenum dithiocarbamate (MoDTC) additives. These additives are widely used in lubricants because they can react at rubbing surfaces to form protective films that reduce wear and, in some cases, friction. The main objective of the work was to better understand how the composition of the lubricant influences the internal structure and mechanical response of the resulting tribofilm.

To characterize these films, the researchers used dynamic nanoindentation experiments combined with stiffness modeling. This approach made it possible to probe the mechanical properties of the tribofilms at very small length scales and to distinguish the response of different layers within the film. By analyzing variations in stiffness with penetration depth, the study provided insight into how the films were organized through their thickness and how their mechanical behavior changed from the surface toward the substrate.

In addition to indentation measurements, local nano-friction experiments were carried out to determine how the friction coefficient varied as a function of applied pressure. These measurements allowed the researchers to compare the frictional response of tribofilms produced from different lubricant formulations, including films formed with MoDTC alone and those formed with a combination of MoDTC and ZDTP.

The films generated from MoDTC alone exhibited relatively low applied pressures, below approximately 0.5 GPa, during the nano-friction tests. Despite the presence of molybdenum-based additive chemistry, these films showed a high apparent friction coefficient, greater than 0.4. This indicates that MoDTC by itself did not produce an optimally lubricating tribofilm under the tested conditions, or that the low-friction molybdenum disulfide structures expected from MoDTC were not sufficiently activated or organized to provide significant friction reduction.

By contrast, tribofilms formed from lubricants containing both MoDTC and ZDTP displayed a distinct low-friction region located a few nanometers below the surface. This very low friction domain was attributed to the formation and sliding of MoS₂ planes. The results suggest that ZDTP plays an important role in enabling the pressure conditions or structural environment needed for these MoS₂ layers to become effective. Under sufficiently high local pressure, the MoS₂ planes can slide easily over one another, producing a marked reduction in friction.

Overall, the study shows that the friction-reducing performance of MoDTC is strongly influenced by the presence of ZDTP. While MoDTC alone may form films with relatively high apparent friction, the combination of MoDTC and ZDTP can generate a layered tribofilm with a mechanically favorable subsurface region that promotes very low friction. These findings highlight the importance of additive interactions in lubricant formulations and demonstrate how nanoscale mechanical and friction measurements can reveal the mechanisms responsible for anti-wear and friction-reducing behavior.
outputs.L4:
Dynamic nanoindentation combined with stiffness modeling and local nano-friction measurements was used to investigate the mechanical and tribological properties of anti-wear tribofilms formed from lubricants containing zinc dialkyldithiophosphate (ZDTP), molybdenum dithiocarbamate (MoDTC), or mixtures of both additives. These techniques made it possible to probe the films at very small length scales and to relate their local mechanical response to their frictional behavior. In particular, the study focused on the layered structure of the tribofilms, their rheological response under contact loading, and the way their friction varied with applied pressure.

The results showed that the tribofilms were not homogeneous surface layers, but rather consisted of distinct mechanical and tribological domains. Dynamic nanoindentation revealed variations in stiffness and viscoelastic behavior through the film thickness, indicating a stratified structure produced during rubbing. By combining these measurements with mechanical modeling, the local response of the film could be separated from that of the underlying substrate, allowing a more accurate description of the tribofilm properties.

Local nano-friction experiments further demonstrated that the frictional behavior depended strongly on both the additive chemistry and the contact pressure. Films generated from MoDTC alone exhibited relatively high friction at low pressure, suggesting that the presence of molybdenum-containing species was not sufficient by itself to produce ultra-low friction under mild local loading conditions. In contrast, when MoDTC was used together with ZDTP, the resulting tribofilms could sustain higher pressures and displayed a markedly different frictional response.

Most importantly, the ZDTP-containing MoDTC tribofilms revealed an ultra-low-friction subsurface region. This low-friction domain was attributed to the formation and favorable orientation of MoS₂ lamellae, whose basal planes acted as easy sliding planes under appropriate pressure conditions. The presence of ZDTP appears to promote or stabilize the tribofilm structure required for this alignment, thereby enabling the activation of the low-friction mechanism associated with MoS₂.

These findings highlight the essential role of ZDTP in controlling the structure and performance of MoDTC-derived tribofilms. Rather than acting only as an anti-wear additive, ZDTP helps create the mechanical and chemical environment necessary for MoDTC to generate an effective low-friction tribofilm. The study therefore shows that the superior friction-reducing performance of combined ZDTP/MoDTC lubricant formulations arises from a pressure-dependent, layered tribofilm architecture in which a subsurface MoS₂-rich domain becomes active under sufficiently high contact stress.
outputs.L5:
The use of ZDTP and MoDTC is important in modern lubricant technology, especially in engine oils and industrial lubricants. ZDTP, or zinc dialkyldithiophosphate, is widely known for its anti-wear and antioxidant properties. It helps protect metal surfaces by forming a protective film that reduces friction and prevents damage under high pressure and temperature conditions.

MoDTC, or molybdenum dithiocarbamate, is commonly used as a friction modifier. It helps improve fuel efficiency by reducing friction between moving parts. When MoDTC decomposes during operation, it can form molybdenum-based compounds on metal surfaces, which provide excellent lubrication and wear protection.

The combination of ZDTP and MoDTC can offer strong performance benefits in lubricants. ZDTP provides reliable wear protection and oxidation stability, while MoDTC contributes to lower friction and improved energy efficiency. However, formulators must carefully balance these additives because their interactions can affect overall lubricant performance.

In modern lubricant formulations, ZDTP and MoDTC remain valuable components for improving durability, efficiency, and protection in mechanical systems.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a scientific abstract describing dynamic nanoindentation and local nano-friction experiments on tribofilms formed from lubricants containing ZDTP and MoDTC additives.
counterfactuals.output:
Dynamic nanoindentation and local nano-friction measurements were performed to characterize the near-surface mechanical and tribological response of tribofilms generated from lubricants containing zinc dialkyldithiophosphate (ZDTP) and molybdenum dithiocarbamate (MoDTC) additives. Tribofilms were formed on steel substrates under boundary lubrication conditions and subsequently examined using depth-controlled nanoindentation and scanning probe–based friction mapping. The dynamic indentation response revealed a heterogeneous layered structure, with a relatively compliant outer region overlying a stiffer, mechanically reinforced interfacial layer. Films derived from ZDTP-containing oils exhibited increased hardness and reduced modulus gradients consistent with the formation of phosphate-rich antiwear layers. In contrast, MoDTC-containing formulations produced surfaces with significantly reduced local friction, attributed to the generation of MoS₂-like lamellar reaction products within or on top of the tribofilm.

Combined ZDTP/MoDTC additive systems showed coupled mechanical and frictional behavior: ZDTP promoted load-bearing and wear-resistant film formation, while MoDTC contributed low-shear interfacial species that lowered nanoscale friction. Local nano-friction measurements demonstrated strong spatial variations in friction coefficient, reflecting chemical and structural heterogeneity within the tribofilm. Regions of low friction were correlated with mechanically softer surface domains, whereas harder phosphate-rich areas provided enhanced resistance to penetration. The results show that dynamic nanoindentation, when combined with high-resolution friction probing, provides a powerful approach for resolving the structure–property relationships of tribochemical films. These findings highlight the complementary roles of ZDTP and MoDTC in controlling boundary lubrication performance through the simultaneous development of protective mechanical layers and low-shear tribological interfaces.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Explain the main findings of a study on the layered structure and friction behavior of anti-wear films generated in rolling/sliding contacts with ZDTP and MoDTC.
counterfactuals.output:
The study found that anti-wear/low-friction films formed from lubricants containing **ZDTP** and **MoDTC** are not uniform coatings, but **chemically and mechanically layered tribofilms** whose structure controls friction.

Main findings:

- **ZDTP forms the main anti-wear film.**  
  In rolling/sliding contact, ZDTP reacts on steel surfaces to produce a relatively thick, patchy tribofilm made mainly of **zinc/iron polyphosphates** with sulphur-containing species. This film protects the steel by separating the surfaces and reducing wear.

- **The tribofilm has a layered structure.**  
  The film is typically stratified:
  - an inner layer close to the steel, often rich in iron sulphides/oxides and short-chain phosphates;
  - a middle/upper phosphate-rich glassy layer containing zinc and phosphorus;
  - surface regions that can contain sulphides and reaction products from friction modifiers.

- **MoDTC provides the low-friction component.**  
  MoDTC decomposes during rubbing to form **molybdenum disulphide, MoS₂**, especially near the outer surface of the tribofilm. MoS₂ has a lamellar crystal structure and shears easily, which gives low friction.

- **Low friction is linked to MoS₂ formation, not simply to film thickness.**  
  The presence of a ZDTP-derived film gives wear protection, but the major friction reduction occurs when MoDTC-derived **MoS₂ sheets** are generated and retained at the sliding interface.

- **ZDTP and MoDTC interact synergistically, but also competitively.**  
  ZDTP helps create a durable surface film on which MoDTC decomposition products can accumulate. However, the chemistry is complex: ZDTP-derived phosphate films can influence how much MoS₂ forms and how stable it is at the surface.

- **The films are heterogeneous.**  
  Rather than being smooth continuous layers, the tribofilms consist of pads or islands with varying thickness, composition, and mechanical properties. This heterogeneity affects local contact pressure, shear, and friction behavior.

- **Friction behavior changes with film evolution.**  
  Initially, friction may be relatively high while the ZDTP anti-wear film develops. As MoDTC decomposes and MoS₂ forms on or within the upper tribofilm, friction falls. If the MoS₂ is consumed, oxidized, or removed, friction can rise again.

In short, the study showed that **ZDTP mainly builds a protective phosphate-based anti-wear tribofilm**, while **MoDTC supplies low friction by forming MoS₂ at the rubbing surface**. The key conclusion is that friction and wear performance are governed by the **layered nanoscale structure and chemistry** of the tribofilm, not just by the presence of additives in the oil.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Produce a technical summary of how ZDTP enables low-friction behavior in MoDTC-containing tribofilms, including pressure ranges and the role of MoS2 planes.
counterfactuals.output:
ZDTP/ZDDP enables low-friction behavior in MoDTC-containing tribofilms mainly by creating the mechanical and chemical conditions needed for MoDTC to form and retain shearable MoS₂ at the rubbing interface.

## Mechanism

- **MoDTC is the friction modifier precursor.** Under rubbing, MoDTC decomposes and forms Mo-containing sulfide/oxide species, ideally **MoS₂**.
- **ZDTP forms a load-bearing antiwear tribofilm**, typically a zinc/iron polyphosphate glass containing ZnS/FeS and other sulfur/phosphorus species.
- This ZDTP-derived film is relatively hard, patchy, and pad-like. It:
  - protects the substrate from severe wear,
  - concentrates local stress at asperity contacts,
  - provides sulfur-containing chemistry that can assist MoS₂ formation,
  - stabilizes MoS₂-rich material near the surface instead of allowing it to be rapidly removed.

## Pressure ranges

In typical boundary-lubricated steel contacts, the nominal Hertzian pressures are often in the range of roughly:

- **0.5–1.5 GPa** for many ball-on-disc or engine-relevant tribometer conditions.

However, because the ZDTP tribofilm is rough and pad-like, the **local asperity contact pressures** can be significantly higher, commonly estimated to reach:

- **~1–3 GPa**, and in some nanoscale contacts potentially higher.

These elevated local pressures are important because they promote tribochemical decomposition of MoDTC and the structural ordering of MoS₂. At too low a pressure, MoDTC decomposition and MoS₂ orientation may be incomplete; at excessively high pressures or severe sliding conditions, MoS₂ can be disrupted, oxidized, or worn away faster than it forms.

## Role of MoS₂ planes

The low-friction state is associated with the formation of **lamellar MoS₂** at the outermost tribofilm surface.

- MoS₂ has a layered crystal structure.
- Strong covalent bonding exists within each S–Mo–S sheet.
- Adjacent sheets are held together mainly by weak van der Waals forces.
- When the **basal planes of MoS₂ become aligned parallel to the sliding direction**, interlayer shear is easy.

Thus, the lowest friction occurs when the tribofilm contains nanoscale MoS₂ sheets with their basal planes lying parallel to the rubbing surface. These planes act as solid-lubricant lamellae, allowing sliding by interlayer shear rather than by shearing the harder ZDTP phosphate matrix or the steel surface.

## Overall picture

ZDTP does not by itself provide very low friction; its main role is to build a durable antiwear scaffold and generate high local contact pressures. In the presence of MoDTC, that scaffold promotes the formation, retention, and orientation of MoS₂. Low friction appears when the contact pressure and sliding conditions are sufficient to produce MoS₂ and align its basal planes parallel to sliding, typically within boundary-lubrication contacts operating around **~0.5–1.5 GPa nominal pressure**, with **local asperity pressures of roughly ~1–3 GPa**.

counterfactuals.prompt: Draft a journal-style abstract on rheological properties and friction coefficients of lubricant-derived tribofilms containing zinc dialkyldithiophosphate and molybdenum dialkyldithiocarbamate.
counterfactuals.output:
**Abstract**

Tribofilms derived from lubricant additives play a central role in controlling friction and wear in boundary-lubricated contacts. In this study, the rheological properties and frictional response of tribofilms formed from zinc dialkyldithiophosphate (ZDDP) and molybdenum dialkyldithiocarbamate (MoDTC) were investigated to clarify the relationship between film composition, shear behavior, and friction reduction. Tribofilms were generated under controlled sliding conditions using lubricant formulations containing ZDDP, MoDTC, and combined ZDDP/MoDTC additive packages. The resulting interfacial layers were examined in terms of nanoscale mechanical response, shear strength, and effective friction coefficient. ZDDP-containing films exhibited relatively high stiffness and shear resistance, consistent with the formation of phosphate-rich antiwear layers. In contrast, MoDTC-containing systems produced low-shear-strength surface species, attributed to molybdenum disulfide-like phases, which reduced the friction coefficient under boundary lubrication. When ZDDP and MoDTC were used together, the tribofilms displayed mixed rheological behavior, combining the load-bearing characteristics of ZDDP-derived phosphate networks with the lubricious response of MoDTC-derived molybdenum sulfide phases. The friction coefficient was strongly dependent on the balance between these mechanically robust and shear-compliant components, indicating that tribofilm rheology governs macroscopic friction performance. These findings highlight the importance of additive-derived tribofilm structure and viscoelastic/shear properties in determining lubricant efficiency and provide insight into the design of advanced low-friction, antiwear lubricant formulations.
